- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. # Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

{"number":1174,"title":"fleet-baseline can only force `update` — there is no lever for any other task fleet-wide","body":"`fleet-baseline` is the fleet's only forcing lever, and it hard-codes what it forces:

```js
// packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-baseline/force-fleet-baseline.mjs
export const FORCED_TASK = 'update';
```

Everything underneath it is already generic — `fireScheduler(gh, fullName, ref, taskId)` takes the id as an argument, and the member-side `planWake` accepts a whitespace/comma-separated list of `task` or `pack/task` ids and *creates* the standing item when one is missing. Only the constant is fixed.

So "force task X across the fleet" has exactly one route today: dispatch each member's `claudinite-scheduler.yml` yourself with `wake: X`. That needs Actions-write on every member, which is the credential `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` exists to hold and which an interactive session scoped to a handful of repos does not have. The alternative — attaching every member to the session — is per-repo manual work, which reliably does not happen.

Surfaced doing #1158's "force `usage-fold` fleet-wide" step. It cost nothing there: the converge `fleet-baseline` forces lands a commit on each member's default branch, and that commit is exactly what `usage-fold`'s movement precondition gates on, so forcing `update` forced the fold one hop later by accident. The next task that wants a fleet-wide force will not be so lucky.

**Shape of the fix** (the lever's `README` already documents the parameter-bag pattern this would join): a `WAKE` context parameter beside the existing `REPOS` / `DRY_RUN` / `INCLUDE_DORMANT`, defaulting to `update` so every existing item keeps its meaning, passed through to `fireScheduler` and named in the run summary. The summary line already reads *"Asked each covered member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` to wake its `update` item"* — it would just stop being a constant.

Two things to get right, both learned the hard way in this repo:

- **The protocol spans repos.** The dispatch input is read by each member's own vendored scheduler stub, so a new spelling has to be one every fielded stub already understands. `wake` itself is unchanged here — only which id travels in it — so this should be safe, but it is the class of change that broke Shepherd's only caller in #929.
- **A parameter that stops being read must fail loudly** (#974). If `WAKE` is added, an item naming a task no declared pack owns must land in the summary's `failed` list, not dispatch `update` silently because the name did not resolve.

Not urgent — nothing is blocked on it — but it is a hole in the fleet's control surface that is invisible until someone needs it.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1174","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["quick-win"],"assignees":[],"comments":1,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-21T15:19:37Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T18:00:17Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":748,"title":"conformance-backlog: committed-build-artifact check (promote cannot land a check — fixtures sit outside its write surface)","body":"Two things, from the 2026-08-11 `canon-curation/growth-promote` run (#745, PR #747).

## 1. A structural block: promote's ladder cannot reach the check rung

`growth-promote`'s task spec says a lesson a check can carry is **authored as the check** in the promote PR — "the rule module in the right pack, the failure message carrying the generalized lesson, **plus a fixture test proving it fires**".

That is mechanically impossible today:

- promote's write surface is bounded to `packs/` and `skills/`, enforced by `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/promote-scope.mjs` on the `growth-promote` branch prefix;
- a canon pack's fixture test lives under `packs-tests/`, which is **outside** that surface;
- and it cannot move into `packs/` either — `.github/workflows/ci.yml` pins a closed set of test roots (`engine-tests/`, `packs-tests/`, `vendoring/`, `dev/tools/`, `.claudinite/local/packs/`), with `engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs` failing on any tracked test outside them.

So every promote run must fall back to prose for a convertible rule, and the "prose is the fallback, not the default" ladder never fires. Whichever way it is resolved (widen `inBounds` to `packs-tests/`, or add `packs/` as a test root), it is an owner decision — the run declined to widen its own gate.

## 2. The conversion this blocked

The `.gitignore`-pruning lesson (LaughCounter's local pack, promoted as prose to `git-github-advanced` in #747) converts to a world-scope `basics` check. Written and green locally before being pulled:

- **`packs/basics/committed-build-artifact.mjs`** — advisory, relevance-first. Flags a *tracked* file matching a confined set of artifacts no project tracks on purpose: `__pycache__/`, `*.py[co]`, `.pytest_cache/`, `.mypy_cache/`, `.ruff_cache/`, `*.egg-info/`, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`. The `fix` line carries the lesson (delete the artifacts before dropping their ignore rules; read `git diff --cached --stat` after a bulk `git add -A`).
- **`packs-tests/basics/committed-build-artifact.test.mjs`** — four cases: clean tree silent; a swept-in `__pycache__` found; the tool-cache/OS set found; and a narrowness case proving silence on deliberately vendored trees (`node_modules/`, `dist/`, `build/`) and on prose merely naming `__pycache__`.

Advisory rather than blocking on purpose: the fix is a deletion, and pre-existing junk in a member repo should surface as a finding to clear, not red that repo's sweep and block its maintenance PR.

The set was chosen so the check stays inert on anything a repo might legitimately vendor; `node_modules/` and `dist/` are deliberately excluded.

Refs #745.

You are triaging a batch of GitHub issues in the repo missingbulb/Claudinite, on behalf of the Claudinite "tidy-issues" automated task. This is real production work — actions taken (closing issues, adding labels, posting comments) are live and visible. Follow the procedure below EXACTLY for each issue in your batch. Use ONLY mcp__github__* tools for GitHub access (issue_read, issue_write, search_code, get_file_contents, list_issues, etc.) — do not use gh CLI, do not touch pull requests (no PR reads/writes: this task's scope is issues only).

You may use mcp__github__get_file_contents with ref: "main" to check whether something described in an issue is actually implemented in main's current content — never infer from a linked PR having merged, never from the issue merely "looking done". You may also use Bash/Grep/Read against the local checkout ONLY as a fallback if it happens to already reflect main (check `git rev-parse HEAD` against `git ls-remote origin main` first); prefer the GitHub API for certainty.

The ladder (apply the FIRST that matches, and take exactly one action per issue):
1. Already implemented in main → close it (issue_write, method update, state: closed, state_reason: completed) + post one comment citing where in main it landed (file/line or behavior). Action = "closed".
2. Conflicts with a current guideline (something documented in this repo's packs/ or CLAUDE.md now contradicts what the issue asks) → add label "needs-decision" (create it if missing) + comment naming the conflict. Action = "needs-decision".
3. Blocked by another issue (explicitly, or structurally can't proceed until another open issue resolves) → add label "blocked" + comment "blocked by #N". Action = "blocked".
4. Small and quick to do (a well-scoped, low-risk, single-file-ish change) → add label "quick-win" + comment scoping it in 1-2 sentences. Action = "quick-win".
5. Else → take no action. Action = "left".

Special rule — ticked checkboxes: if EVERY checkbox in the issue body is ticked, that's the author's own claim the work is done. Treat it as a strong reason to run the "implemented in main" check (step 1), never as the answer by itself. If verified true against main → close as in step 1. If NOT verified → post a comment naming specifically what's still missing (do NOT close). Action = "left" for this comment-only sub-case (say in your note that you commented). If the ask has no repo-side artifact (e.g. a console/GitHub setting only a human can flip) — the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition: say so in the comment and close (Action = "closed"). A PARTIALLY ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage as if no boxes existed.

Never re-post a verdict you already posted: before acting, read the issue's comments (issue_read, method get_comments). Find the most recent comment that ends with a line `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->` (or, for an issue triaged before this marker existed, one that clearly reads as this task's own prior verdict). If the action you are about to take is the SAME as that comment's already-announced verdict, do NOT post anything and do NOT change any label — return action = "unchanged", note = "<action> since <its date>". Closing is never a repeat (it changes state), so if a prior verdict said e.g. "quick-win" and you'd now close it, that's a real new action, not unchanged.

End every comment you post with this exact marker, alone on the last line:
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
(substitute the actual action word: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left)

Your batch of issues to triage in missingbulb/Claudinite: #840, #996, #1003, #991, #766, #952, #223, #920

For EACH issue, do the full read (get + get_comments + get_labels), decide, act, and record. When done with all issues in your batch, report back a compact list, one line per issue, in EXACTLY this format:
#<n>: action=<closed|needs-decision|blocked|quick-win|left|unchanged> — <one-sentence note, and if you closed/commented/labeled, say what you did>

Do not touch any issue outside your assigned batch. Do not touch any pull request. Do not modify this repo's tracker issues (titled "Claudinite tracker: Tidy Issues" or "Claudinite tracker: Repo Tidy") — that reconciliation is handled separately by the orchestrating session, not by you.

You may also use Bash/Grep/Read against the local checkout ONLY as a fallback if it happens to already reflect main (check `git rev-parse HEAD` against `git ls-remote origin main` first); prefer the GitHub API for certainty.

The ladder (apply the FIRST that matches, and take exactly one action per issue):
1. Already implemented in main → close it (issue_write, method update, state: closed, state_reason: completed) + post one comment citing where in main it landed (file/line or behavior). Action = "closed".
2. Conflicts with a current guideline (something documented in this repo's packs/ or CLAUDE.md now contradicts what the issue asks) → add label "needs-decision" (create it if missing) + comment naming the conflict. Action = "needs-decision".
3. Blocked by another issue (explicitly, or structurally can't proceed until another open issue resolves) → add label "blocked" + comment "blocked by #N". Action = "blocked".
4. Small and quick to do (a well-scoped, low-risk, single-file-ish change) → add label "quick-win" + comment scoping it in 1-2 sentences. Action = "quick-win".
5. Else → take no action. Action = "left".

Special rule — ticked checkboxes: if EVERY checkbox in the issue body is ticked, that's the author's own claim the work is done. Treat it as a strong reason to run the "implemented in main" check (step 1), never as the answer by itself. If verified true against main → close as in step 1. If NOT verified → post a comment naming specifically what's still missing (do NOT close). Action = "left" for this comment-only sub-case (say in your note that you commented). If the ask has no repo-side artifact (e.g. a console/GitHub setting only a human can flip) — the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition: say so in the comment and close (Action = "closed"). A PARTIALLY ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage as if no boxes existed.

Never re-post a verdict you already posted: before acting, read the issue's comments (issue_read, method get_comments). Find the most recent comment that ends with a line `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->` (or, for an issue triaged before this marker existed, one that clearly reads as this task's own prior verdict). If the action you are about to take is the SAME as that comment's already-announced verdict, do NOT post anything and do NOT change any label — return action = "unchanged", note = "<action> since <its date>". Closing is never a repeat (it changes state), so if a prior verdict said e.g. "quick-win" and you'd now close it, that's a real new action, not unchanged.

End every comment you post with this exact marker, alone on the last line:
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
(substitute the actual action word: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left)

Your batch of issues to triage in missingbulb/Claudinite: #840, #996, #1003, #991, #766, #952, #223, #920

For EACH issue, do the full read (get + get_comments + get_labels), decide, act, and record. When done with all issues in your batch, report back a compact list, one line per issue, in EXACTLY this format:
#<n>: action=<closed|needs-decision|blocked|quick-win|left|unchanged> — <one-sentence note, and if you closed/commented/labeled, say what you did>

Do not touch any issue outside your assigned batch. Do not touch any pull request. Do not modify this repo's tracker issues (titled "Claudinite tracker: Tidy Issues" or "Claudinite tracker: Repo Tidy") — that reconciliation is handled separately by the orchestrating session, not by you.

{"number":1224,"title":"Eliminate avoidable GitHub-platform assumptions from packs","body":"A census of GitHub-platform assumptions (the platform, not plain git) across the engine and every pack found 367 distinct assumptions counted once per component — 81 in the engine, 286 across the packs.

Scoping this work to the packs, and excluding `git-github` (which owns GitHub as a subject, 38 assumptions), leaves ~248 in scope. Of those, roughly 40–50 are avoidable and fall in two buckets:

**Bucket 1 — not actually GitHub assumptions (~13).** Generic-CI facts phrased in GitHub vocabulary, which the census counts only because the wording names a GitHub feature. They hold on any CI system:

- `firebase` (4) — "release-workflow variables", "workflow dispatch"
- `web-scraping` (3) — runner IP blocks, "repository secrets", commit-step durability
- `macos` (2) — secret-gated signing lane, build annotations
- `spec-driven-product` (2) — CI-gated merge, automated release cut
- `aws-sam` (1) — deploy-workflow staleness caveat
- `research-project` (1) — branch/commit/PR conventions

The fix is a phrasing pass to platform-neutral wording. No behavior changes.

**Bucket 2 — restatements of facts another pack or skill owns (~25–30).** These violate the corpus's own dependency rule ("say what A needs from B; don't re-spell how B does its job"). Repeat offenders:

- "`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/`" — re-explained in `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `claudinite-lifecycle` when the engine's withhold lane owns it
- "`GITHUB_TOKEN` pushes fire no workflows" — re-derived in `claudinite-dashboard`, `chrome-extension`, `static-website` when `git-github` owns it
- the exact-title-tracker / issue-creation-lands-open / no-comment-update-tool cluster — owned by the `unattended-agents` skill, restated in `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`
- squash-merge evidence rules — owned by `git-github`, restated in `basics` and `tidy-repo` skills

Two exemptions constrain this bucket: vendored workflow stubs must stay self-contained (their comments travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles), and `task.md` files are read standalone by executor sessions, so some restatement there is deliberate context rather than drift.

**Out of scope.** The remaining ~200 are inherent — the dashboard's rate-limit/OAuth/Pages model, sheepdog's fleet API vocabulary, lifecycle's PR delivery, growth's issue-queue semantics, the two vendored release pipelines, basics' issue→PR lifecycle, tidy-repo's triage primitives. Eliminating those means dropping the capability or building a forge-abstraction seam, neither of which is justified without a second consumer. The per-pack REST-client duplication is likewise deliberate (#959).

[{"id":5379959696,"body":"## Finding: the elimination premise does not survive contact with the files

I read every candidate site rather than working from the census summaries. **Close to none of the ~40–50 is safely eliminable.** The estimate in the issue body was derived from sweep summaries, which record *that* a pack asserts a GitHub fact but not *whether* the assertion is gratuitous. Reading them in context, almost every one is either already platform-neutral or load-bearing.

### Bucket 1 was largely a census artifact, not prose to fix

The sweeps counted the *concept* landing on Actions in practice, not GitHub vocabulary in the text. Checked line by line:

| Site | Text | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `firebase/skills/create-release-plan/SKILL.md:28,30` | "release-workflow variables", "the release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset" | already neutral |
| `macos/RULES.md:64,77` | "signing secrets being present", "in a build annotation" | already neutral |
| `spec-driven-product/RULES.md:56,127` | "gate the merge from CI", "cuts from `main`" | already neutral |
| `aws-sam/RULES.md:17` | "the last green deploy workflow" | already neutral |
| `web-scraping/RULES.md:59,154` | datacenter-IP blocks, commit-step durability | already neutral |
| `research-project/RULES.md:380` | "branch/commit/PR conventions" | cross-forge |

Genuine edits available: **1–2 marginal ones** (`firebase:50` "a workflow dispatch", `web-scraping:55` "repository secrets"), each worth one census point and each slightly *less* precise afterward. `macos/README.md:63` names GitHub Actions in a **provenance** note about a real project that genuinely used it — vaguening a factual attribution makes the doc worse, not more portable.

### Bucket 2: every candidate has a legitimate defense

- **Vendored stubs** (`chrome-extension`, `static-website` bump-version workflows) travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles. Must stay self-contained.
- **Migration records** (`claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` ×2) are dated historical accounts. The canon says do not change historical records.
- **`task.md` files** (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`) are read standalone by executor sessions.
- **The canary README** — the fact *is* the pack's reason to exist.
- **`claudinite-dashboard`** (`README.md:498`, `pack.mjs:37`) states the fact as the **premise** of a design decision (seed the workflow; follow the scheduler rather than `push`). It does not re-spell the withhold mechanism, and the canon rule permits A to say what it needs from B.
- **Squash-merge "restatements"** turned out not to exist: `basics` has none, and `tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md:11` is a six-word parenthetical justifying its own decision rule.

### The always-loaded surface is already clean

`RULES.md` is the only text every session in every declaring repo pays for, and it is already lean: `tidy-repo/RULES.md` has **zero** GitHub mentions despite 11 credited assumptions (they live in skills and `task.mjs`, where they belong), and `basics/RULES.md`'s nine are the issue→branch→PR lifecycle itself, already delegating procedure to `git-github-advanced`.

### One genuinely ambiguous case, resolved against editing

`writing-tasks/SKILL.md:171` says `task.md` must state the **constraint** and drop the mechanism. The tracker cluster's "creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument" is mechanism by that reading — but it is precisely what stops a session collapsing the two calls into one. Dropping it trades a census point for a live failure mode.

### Recommendation

**Do not run the sweep.** Landing ~40 edits to hit a number would vaguen accurate provenance, weaken standalone-readable task specs, and rewrite historical migration records — a net loss against a metric that was never a cost. The ~200 inherent assumptions are what these packs *do*; the only real lever is a forge-abstraction seam, which #959's standing decision rejects absent a second consumer.

No code changes pushed. Awaiting a decision on whether to close this as not-planned.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/single-issue-triage

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

One risk this issue carries implicitly is now retired. The acceptance probe — "purge all release aspects from MissingBulbWebsite so it simulates a fresh repo, adopt the pack, and the first release works on the first go" — depends on `static-website`'s `static-site-vendoring` record materializing four workflows into the repo's own `.github/workflows/`. Nor had **any** record: a `materialize` whose `dest` is under `.github/workflows/` had never run against a live member, which is the residual #649 was reopened for. It is not a benign untested path — the update flow commits with the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, GitHub refuses it there, and the refusal rejects the *whole ref*. A broken lane would have failed the first adopter's entire converge, and the acceptance probe would have been the thing that discovered it.

Verified end to end on the canary on 2026-08-14 (evidence on #649), through the same `write` `static-site-vendoring` uses: withheld to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, carried in the PR, parked at `apply-stage`, moved into `.github/workflows/` byte-for-byte by a session, staging swept.

So the vendoring half of the adoption path is no longer an unknown going into this work. One caveat found in the same run and worth knowing before the probe is timed: the apply stage did not merge its own PR, so delivery waited for the next cycle's disposal — on a daily `update`, up to 24h. Fix in #832; without it, "the first release works on the first go" could look like a failure that is really a wait.

The design's open questions, lifted out of `DESIGN.md` so they are decidable here rather than inside a merged doc. Nothing is decided or changed by this comment.

The design landed in #723. Three questions it deliberately left to the owner:

### 1. Pack name — `static-website` or `github-pages-serving`?

Cosmetic. The task framing called for a "github-pages-serving pack", but the pack owns versioning and the CI gate as well as the Pages deploy, so the broader name is arguably the more accurate one. **Default if unanswered: keep `static-website`** — renaming costs a vendored-path migration across adopters and buys nothing the id doesn't already say.

### 2. EdFringeNow data refreshes — `deploy-only`, or full releases?

This is the one with a live consequence, and **as adopted neither behaviour is happening**. EdFringeNow's #319 states the expectation that hourly refreshes keep cutting releases ("roughly 17/day"). They don't: the refresh task runs inside the scheduler workflow and pushes with its `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which fires no `push` event, so the release orchestrator never starts.

Confirmed against the repo since adoption:

- `bb3089c` (2026-08-12 05:22Z, "Refresh Fringe data (daily top-up)" — a scheduler-authored push into the publish set) cut **no release**. The data went live 7.5 hours later, carried incidentally by `v1.60812.1`, which was triggered by a human PR merge.
- Four releases in the five days since adoption, against five version bumps on the single day before it.
- Nothing has landed in `data/` since that release, so the live site is not stale *right now* — the gap has bitten once, visibly, rather than continuously. The daily-instead-of-hourly change (EdFringeNow #340) narrows the exposure but does not touch the cause.

So the question is not "which cadence do we prefer" but "what should a data push do", and either answer needs wiring that doesn't exist yet:

- **`deploy-only`** (the design's D5/D6 recommendation): the refresh task dispatches the release workflow in a mode that assembles and deploys the current tip without bumping, tagging, or cutting a Release. Fresh data reaches the site; tags keep naming content releases.
- **Full releases per data push**: same dispatch wiring, no new mode — accept a tag + GitHub Release per refresh (~1/day at the current cadence, ~17/day if hourly returns next festival).

Doing nothing keeps today's behaviour, where data reaches the site only when unrelated content ships.

### 3. The public beacon token — commit it, or keep `build_vars`?

The design's D3 argues each site should commit its Cloudflare Web Analytics token directly and delete the injection machinery: the token ships to every visitor in the page, so the repo variable protects nothing, and what it buys (rotation without a commit; forks not inheriting live analytics) is thin against a config key, an exporter, a drift guard, a placeholder convention and a per-repo injection script.

The fleet has since answered the other way in practice — #729's `build_vars` is merged and live on EdFringeNow. It is a well-built mechanism and strictly better than the wholesale export it replaced (#626, closed): a declared list keeps repo vocabulary out of the copy-verbatim stubs, fail-on-unset stops a deleted variable from silently shipping a beaconless site, and being handed only the `vars` context means a secret structurally cannot reach the build.

The design still recommends D3, on the grounds that `build_vars` can carry *only* non-secret values by construction — and any value safe to put in a repo variable is safe to commit — so every possible use of the key has a simpler equivalent in source. **If D3 is accepted, a follow-on question:** retire the `build_vars` capability from the pack once its only user is gone, or keep it dormant for a future build-time value that genuinely varies per environment?

{"number":1072,"title":"Production code must not reference its tests — land it as a check","body":"Owner decision while landing #1066: **there shouldn't be references to tests from production code.** That change removed the four citations it created; the rule itself is still unwritten, and eleven pre-existing sites still cross the line.

## The rule

A shipping `.mjs` under `packs/` or `engine/` must not name a `*.test.mjs` path. It is deterministic, so it belongs on the ladder as a **check**, not prose — the assurance authored and seen to fail before the sites are cleaned.

Documentation is a separate question and probably outside it: `engine/checks/README.md` describing where a pack's tests live, or `.github/workflows/ci.yml` naming test globs, is the corpus documenting itself, not production code pointing at its own test.

## The sites as of today

```
engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs:103
engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs:72
engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs:3
engine/scheduler/run.mjs:10
engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs:35
engine/scheduler/slots.mjs:18
packs/claudinite-dashboard/model.mjs:11
packs/claudinite-dashboard/tasks/fleet-digest/dated-fixture-collision.mjs:4
packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs:14, :36
packs/claudinite-lifecycle/rules-index-current.mjs:26, :51
```

Most say the same thing — "a guard pins this" — and lose nothing by naming the guard rather than its file, which is how the four in #1066 were resolved.

## Why it is not folded into #1066

Cleaning these touches three more pack directories, so it re-delivers `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-growth` and `claudinite-lifecycle` on their version bumps. That restructure's whole constraint was that members see nothing, so the sweep is its own change.

## Where the check lives

`.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/` if it is a canon-corpus rule, or a shared pack if it should reach members — worth deciding first, since the second choice makes it every member's rule and a much wider first run.

{"number":1010,"title":"Ad-hoc tasks: let the owner mark an issue for Claude to implement","body":"## The problem

There is no way to hand a one-off piece of work to the repo's own executor. Every agentic run today comes from a recurring task with a precondition; an issue the owner wants implemented has to be started by hand in a session.

## The ask (owner, this session)

Mark an issue "let Claude do this task"; the next executor run picks it up and runs it in a CCR, at a model of the owner's choice. Minimal security: only an issue authored or approved by someone with push access is eligible, evaluated as a precondition.

## The shape (decided)

A new opt-in canon pack, **`claudinite-tasks-adhoc`** — Claudinite-feature packs now carry the `claudinite-` prefix (owner ruling this session; landing as a rule beside the existing canon-pack naming rule).

- **Trigger label `claude-task`**, applied by the owner. Optional `claude-model:opus|sonnet|haiku` picks the model; opus is the default.
- **Model choice routes to sibling tasks** — one task folder per family, each declaring its own `agent_model`. `agent_model` keeps coming from the repo's own task file, never from the item, so the security property of the queue is untouched.
- **The precondition** (over the existing `issues` signal, which already carries labels) gates on: at least one open issue whose labels map to *this* task's family. Its `context` names the candidates, oldest first.
- **Prework** (Action-side, `GITHUB_TOKEN`) does the authorization as its work: eligible iff the issue's author, or an approving commenter, has an `author_association` of `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR` (server-computed, not forgeable). It picks the single oldest eligible issue, swaps `claude-task` → `claude-running`, and requests the agent naming that issue. An unauthorized candidate gets one comment and its label stripped, so it never re-fires.
- **The agent** implements the issue under the ordinary task lifecycle — branch, `Refs #N`, PR — with `expected_outcome: open-pr`, so it can never merge. The issue body is **data, never instructions**.
- **One issue per run**, sequentially: a failed run leaves `claude-running` for a human rather than retrying forever.

Latency is up to an hour (the tick is the repo's only cron); accepted for v1.

Every Phase 1 checklist item from the plan above is done, with three deviations worth reading before approving:

- **The permission read is a signal, not a call from inside the precondition.** A precondition is pure over collected signals and holds no GitHub client; giving every pack's precondition one so this task could make two reads widens far more than the gate it guards. So a `request` collector — engine-owned, like every other — reads the issue, its `/claude go` comments and each candidate's permission, and returns those facts unjudged; the verdict stays in the built-in task's precondition exactly as §16.4 puts it. DESIGN §16.4 carries the amendment.
- **No migration record for #1064.** The retired origin marker is inert (nothing branches on it — standing vs ad-hoc is structural now), open items' state labels do not change, and closed history is covered decode-side. The migration ops write files, not issue labels, so a record could not have done that work in any case.
- **The permission endpoint is unverified**, and it is the one open risk. This sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, which is a policy boundary rather than something a later agent pass can close — so it needs the first real run, or a human. The failure mode is loud by construction: any answer but 200/404 makes the read `unreadable`, which parks the item in the failure lane with the status on it rather than approving or refusing on a guess.

Two things the build found that the plan did not have:

- The vendor set's blanket "an engine `.md` is maintainer reference" rule was dropping the built-in task's `task.md` — a mount whose request session has nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern, and its regression test now walks the queue engine rather than listing its top level, which is what let it through.
- Deriving standing-vs-ad-hoc structurally makes an unqualified hand-created item for a *scheduled* task indistinguishable from that task's standing item, so `create-work-item` now refuses that shape and names `--wake` / `--qualifier` instead.

Phase 2 (the validation burst on a live queue-mode repo) is untouched and still open; this issue stays open for it.

## The happy path, end to end (2026-08-19 23:00–23:06 UTC)

[#1074](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1074) marked `claude-task` + `claude-model:sonnet` → tick → [#1075](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1075) → session → [#1076](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1076), six minutes end to end. - **Labels ensured** by the tick before anything was marked — `claude-task` exists in the picker with its colour and description.
- **Adoption**: item titled `[claudinite-work] engine/implement-request #1074`, body `Request: #1074` / `Model: sonnet`, born `task:ready`. Both marks consumed, `claude-queued` on, one comment naming the item and the family.
- **Pickup**: precondition passed, claim + hand-off + one session, item to `task:agent`.

- **Converge**: item parked open at `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-approval`; #1074 swapped `claude-queued` → `claude-in-review` with the PR and the model named.

**The permission API answers under the executor workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`.** That was the open risk — the sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, so it could not be settled at landing. A failed read would have parked #1075 at `task:needs-human-failure` with the status on it; instead the verdict passed on the read. No workflow permission needed adding.

The item's Context rendered as two near-identical bullets — adoption writes one, the precondition added another — in the one section the session is told to read as its binding scope. [#1077](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1077) drops the precondition's.

## Still not verified, and why

The **unauthorized-mark refusal** (the plan's second Phase 2 trace). It needs an issue whose author has no push access here; every identity available to this session is the owner's, so it cannot be staged, and the adoption→pickup window the withdrawal variant would need is seconds wide (the drain follows the tick in the same run). The engine tests cover both shapes against the real executor with a fake GitHub — S45's disarm and S48's withdrawal — but the live trace is a human's to produce, from a second account, and it is the one thing left on this issue.

{"number":1078,"title":"Human-only: trace the request mode refusing an unauthorized mark, live","body":"The last unverified path of the ad-hoc request mode (#1010, landed in [#1067](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1067)). It needs a **second GitHub account with no push access on this repository**, which no session has, so it is yours.

The happy path is already traced live ([#1074](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1074) → [#1075](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1075) → [#1076](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1076), 2026-08-19) and that run confirmed the permission API answers under the executor's `GITHUB_TOKEN`. What it did **not** exercise is the branch taken for somebody who is not a collaborator at all: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{login}/permission` answering **404**, which the engine reads as "no permission" rather than as a failed read.

## Why it is worth the ten minutes

That 404 is the difference between the two things this mode must never confuse:

- read as `none` → the request is **refused** and disarmed, which is the design;
- read as a failed read → the run **parks** in the failure lane, and every stranger's marked issue becomes a triage item somebody has to clear.

Both are covered by engine tests against a fake GitHub (S45, S46, S50 in `engine-tests/scheduler/queue/request-mode.test.mjs`). Neither has been seen against the real API, and the two differ by one status code.

## Steps

- [ ] **From the second account** (no push access here), open a throwaway issue — anything, one line. *While this is off: nothing to mark.*
- [ ] **From your own account**, apply `claude-task` to it. Applying the mark to somebody else's issue is meant to authorize nothing — that is the point of the trace. *While this is off: the tick has nothing to adopt.*
- [ ] **Run the tick** — wait for the hourly one, or dispatch [Claudinite scheduler](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml) with no inputs. *While this is off: the mark just sits there.*
- [ ] **Watch, on the throwaway issue**: one comment beginning "Not implementing this:", `claude-queued` removed, **no session started**. And on the work item the tick created: closed, `task:obsolete`.
- [ ] **Watch the next tick or two**: nothing re-adopts it. The disarm is what stops the refusal repeating forever.
- [ ] **Second variant, same issue**: have the second account comment `/claude go`, re-apply `claude-task`, run the tick. It must refuse again — the phrase decides nothing; the permission behind it does.
- [ ] **Positive control**: comment `/claude go` yourself, re-apply `claude-task`, run the tick. This one must run. (Skip if you would rather not spend a session; the happy path is already traced.)

## Closing condition

Both refusals observed, with the item numbers linked here, and the throwaway issue closed. If either refusal instead **parks** the item at `task:needs-human-failure`, do not close this — the 404 is being read as a failed read, and the fix is in the `request` collector's `permissionOf` (`engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs`).

You are triaging a batch of GitHub issues in the repo missingbulb/Claudinite, on behalf of the Claudinite "tidy-issues" automated task. This is real production work — actions taken (closing issues, adding labels, posting comments) are live and visible. Follow the procedure below EXACTLY for each issue in your batch. Use ONLY mcp__github__* tools for GitHub access (issue_read, issue_write, search_code, get_file_contents, list_issues, etc.) — do not use gh CLI, do not touch pull requests (no PR reads/writes: this task's scope is issues only).

You may use mcp__github__get_file_contents with ref: "main" to check whether something described in an issue is actually implemented in main's current content — never infer from a linked PR having merged, never from the issue merely "looking done". You may also use Bash/Grep/Read against the local checkout ONLY as a fallback if it happens to already reflect main (check `git rev-parse HEAD` against `git ls-remote origin main` first); prefer the GitHub API for certainty.

The ladder (apply the FIRST that matches, and take exactly one action per issue):
1. Already implemented in main → close it (issue_write, method update, state: closed, state_reason: completed) + post one comment citing where in main it landed (file/line or behavior). Action = "closed".
2. Conflicts with a current guideline (something documented in this repo's packs/ or CLAUDE.md now contradicts what the issue asks) → add label "needs-decision" (create it if missing) + comment naming the conflict. Action = "needs-decision".
3. Blocked by another issue (explicitly, or structurally can't proceed until another open issue resolves) → add label "blocked" + comment "blocked by #N". Action = "blocked".
4. Small and quick to do (a well-scoped, low-risk, single-file-ish change) → add label "quick-win" + comment scoping it in 1-2 sentences. Action = "quick-win".
5. Else → take no action. Action = "left".

Special rule — ticked checkboxes: if EVERY checkbox in the issue body is ticked, that's the author's own claim the work is done. Treat it as a strong reason to run the "implemented in main" check (step 1), never as the answer by itself. If verified true against main → close as in step 1. If NOT verified → post a comment naming specifically what's still missing (do NOT close). Action = "left" for this comment-only sub-case (say in your note that you commented). If the ask has no repo-side artifact (e.g. a console/GitHub setting only a human can flip) — the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition: say so in the comment and close (Action = "closed"). A PARTIALLY ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage as if no boxes existed.

Never re-post a verdict you already posted: before acting, read the issue's comments (issue_read, method get_comments). Find the most recent comment that ends with a line `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->` (or, for an issue triaged before this marker existed, one that clearly reads as this task's own prior verdict). If the action you are about to take is the SAME as that comment's already-announced verdict, do NOT post anything and do NOT change any label — return action = "unchanged", note = "<action> since <its date>". Closing is never a repeat (it changes state), so if a prior verdict said e.g. "quick-win" and you'd now close it, that's a real new action, not unchanged.

End every comment you post with this exact marker, alone on the last line:
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
(substitute the actual action word: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left)

Your batch of issues to triage in missingbulb/Claudinite: #923, #926, #239, #841, #409, #498

For EACH issue, do the full read (get + get_comments + get_labels), decide, act, and record. When done with all issues in your batch, report back a compact list, one line per issue, in EXACTLY this format:
#<n>: action=<closed|needs-decision|blocked|quick-win|left|unchanged> — <one-sentence note, and if you closed/commented/labeled, say what you did>

Do not touch any issue outside your assigned batch. Do not touch any pull request. Do not modify this repo's tracker issues (titled "Claudinite tracker: Tidy Issues" or "Claudinite tracker: Repo Tidy") — that reconciliation is handled separately by the orchestrating session, not by you.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). The ceilings, from [GitHub's docs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api):

| credential | limit |
|---|---|
| unauthenticated | 60/hr per IP |
| user token (PAT, OAuth, GitHub App user token) | 5,000/hr, shared across every app acting for that user |
| GitHub App installation token | 5,000/hr min, up to 12,500 by fleet size |
| Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` | 1,000/hr per repository |

There is no higher tier available to a page that runs as the viewer — 5,000/hr is the ceiling, and it is 83× what the deployment gets today. **The whole fix is configuring `clientId` + `exchangeUrl`** so the sign-in button exists.

- until then, say so in the page: an anonymous viewer must be told what their 60/hour means and that their github.com session is not a credential.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/single-issue-triage

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

{"number":1003,"title":"Manual: register this fleet owner's GitHub App and deploy its token exchange","body":"Four steps no Action can take — they need a credential and a console. Until all four are done the dashboard runs **unauthenticated at 60 requests/hour per IP**, which one fleet sweep exceeds. Context in #996.

**Scope: once per fleet *owner*, not once per fleet — and not once for everybody.** One App and one exchange endpoint serve every deployment *you* own. A GitHub App carries [up to 10 callback URLs](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/registering-a-github-app/about-the-user-authorization-callback-url), and with **wildcard matching** a single callback of `https://.github.io/` covers every project Pages site under that host — so a new Shepherd for a new fleet of yours adds no callback at all, just the two config keys.

Somebody else adopting this pack cannot inherit it, for mechanical reasons: a private App "can only be installed on the account that owns the app. Only members of the organization that owns it can authorize it", and even a public one yields a user token that "can only access resources that both the user and app can access" — so until they install it themselves their whole fleet reads *not visible to you*, and their tokens would be minted by someone else's endpoint. They register their own, or use the token box. Spelled out in the pack README (#1007).

- [ ] **Register a GitHub App** ([new App](https://github.com/settings/apps/new)) with read-only **Contents**, **Issues** and **Actions**, and *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation* enabled. Callback URL: the deployed dashboard's page URL — or the `https://.github.io/` root with **Enable wildcard matching** ticked, which covers every future deployment on that host. Note the **client ID**, generate a **client secret**.
  - *while undone:* no sign-in button exists; every viewer is anonymous.
- [ ] **Install the App** on the account holding the fleet's repos ([installations](https://github.com/settings/installations)). Once per *account*, not per repo — a new repo under an installed account is covered by "all repositories", or added to the selection.
  - *while undone:* sign-in succeeds but the token can read nothing, so every member row reads "not visible to you".
- [ ] **Deploy the exchange** — [`oauth-exchange.example.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/claudinite-dashboard/oauth-exchange.example.mjs) as-is to a worker, with the client ID and secret as its environment. One deployment serves every dashboard you own, since it holds that App's secret and nothing else.
  - *while undone:* clicking sign-in returns to a page that cannot finish, and says the exchange was unreachable.
- [ ] **Set `clientId` and `exchangeUrl`** on the deployment's `claudinite-dashboard` entry in its `.claudinite-checks.json`. Either alone does nothing — the pair is what turns sign-in on. This is the one step a new fleet of yours repeats, with the same two values.
  - *while undone:* nothing changes; the page keeps falling back to the token box.

**Closing condition:** the deployed dashboard shows *Sign in with GitHub*, one authorization gets a viewer through a full fleet sweep, and the rate pill reads `…/5000 · user`.

### Why the exchange cannot be skipped

Verified against the [authorizing-OAuth-apps docs](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps):

- the web flow's token exchange lists `client_secret` as **Required**, flatly — GitHub supports PKCE (`code_challenge`, S256 only) but as *additional* protection, not as a public-client mode that drops the secret;
- the device flow genuinely needs no secret ("The `client_secret` is not needed for the device flow") but it POSTs to `github.com/login/device/code` and `github.com/login/oauth/access_token`, and those are cross-origin for a page on `github.io`. The docs state "CORS pre-flight requests (OPTIONS) are not supported at this time"; a browser cannot read a response that carries no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` either. *(The response headers of the token endpoint could not be probed from this sandbox — the proxy denies it — so that last half is documented, not measured here.)*

A browser extension is the case where this *does* work without a server, which is why the Chrome extension flow felt server-free: an extension with host permissions is not subject to the page's CORS rules, so it can call the token endpoint itself. A static page has no such exemption.

This is not a wider credential in each member repo — the App acts as whoever signed in, with exactly their own permissions.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1003","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-18T14:14:11Z","updated_at":"2026-08-18T15:02:49Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1335,"title":"Ship the tasks pack in the engine lane while the legacy shims name it","body":"The live canary caught this on #1326's merge commit, and nothing in the suite could have.

Closes #1334

## What broke

The engine and pack lanes deliver on separate cycles. The `engine/scheduler/` shims are engine-lane files that re-export a pack, so a member converging its engine first held a shim pointing at a pack its mount did not carry yet — the old dashboard version it still had imports `engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs` by name, the shim resolved to nothing, the pack failed to load, and the self-test gate refused to land the converge. Which also meant the member could not receive the pack that would have fixed it.

## The fix

A shim and its target are one unit, so the lane that ships one ships the other: `isEngineFile` carries `packs/claudinite-tasks/` for as long as the shims exist. It comes out with them in [#1329](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1329).

## The test that was missing

It asserts the invariant rather than this instance: **every import in the engine lane must resolve inside the engine lane.** Neither existing guard could see the defect — the fielded-import scan asks whether a path resolves in the canon, which it did, and the rehearsal fixtures are all built from the current canon, so none of them holds the older pack version that makes the window visible. Seen to fail without the fix.

## Verified against the real canary, not a fixture

Cloned `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary` and ran the actual flows:

- `engineUpdate` → `ok`, converged tree passes its self-test (it failed here before the fix)
- `packUpdate` → `ok`, and the declaration now carries `claudinite-tasks`, seeded by the migration record
- the member's own vendored `check_the_world` → exit 0
- the exact `run:` line its workflow carries — `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs` — executes **as the program** through the shim and prints its run report, which is the L2-window risk closed
